questions.q: You're about to move off from the side of the road. What should you do last, just before pulling away?
options: Look round to check your blind spot
Rev the engine to warn pedestrians
questions.explain: Mirrors don't show everything. A final look over your shoulder covers the blind spot where a cyclist or car may be hidden. Only move off when it's safe.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway and start to feel tired. What should you do?
options: Leave at the next exit and find a safe place to stop and rest
Stop on the hard shoulder for a short sleep
Open the window and keep going to your destination
Speed up so the journey ends sooner
questions.explain: The hard shoulder is for emergencies only. Fresh air helps only briefly. Leave the motorway, stop somewhere safe and rest.

questions.q: On a long journey, how often does The Highway Code recommend taking a break?
options: At least 15 minutes after every two hours of driving
Only when you start to feel sleepy
questions.explain: Rule 91 recommends a minimum break of at least 15 minutes after every two hours of driving.

questions.q: When are you allowed to use a hand-held mobile phone while driving?
options: To call 999 or 112 in a genuine emergency when it's unsafe or impractical to stop
When you're stopped in a traffic queue
When the call will be very short
When you're using it as a sat-nav
questions.explain: You must not use a hand-held phone for any purpose while driving, and that includes sitting in queuing traffic. The only exception is a genuine emergency call to 999 or 112 when it's unsafe or impractical to stop.

questions.q: Why can a hands-free phone call still be dangerous while driving?
options: It takes your attention away from the road
It interferes with the car's brakes
questions.explain: Hands-free calls are legal, but the conversation still distracts you. If you aren't in proper control of the vehicle you can still be prosecuted.

questions.q: You want to enter a new destination into your sat-nav partway through a journey. What should you do?
options: Find a safe, legal place to stop first
Do it while waiting at red traffic lights
Do it on a straight, quiet road
Ask a passenger to steer while you type
questions.explain: Reading or typing on a screen takes your eyes and mind off the road. Stop safely first.

questions.q: What is the only reason The Highway Code gives for flashing your headlights?
options: To let other road users know you're there
To let another driver pull out
To warn of a police speed check
questions.explain: Don't flash your headlights to send any other message. The other driver may misread it and pull out into danger.

questions.q: A driver behind you is following much too closely. What should you do?
options: Gradually ease off and leave a bigger gap in front of you
Brake sharply to make them back off
Speed up to get away from them
Close up to the vehicle in front
questions.explain: A larger gap ahead means you can brake more gently and earlier, so the tailgater is less likely to hit you. Don't react aggressively.

questions.q: In a built-up area, between which times must you NOT use your horn (unless another road user poses a danger)?
questions.explain: You must not use your horn while stationary, or when driving in a built-up area between 11.30pm and 7.00am, unless another road user poses a danger.

questions.q: Under the 'hierarchy of road users', who has the greatest responsibility to reduce danger to others?
options: Those in charge of vehicles that can cause the greatest harm
questions.explain: Drivers of larger and heavier vehicles carry the greatest responsibility to look out for and reduce danger to more vulnerable road users.

questions.q: You're turning left into a side road and a pedestrian is waiting to cross it. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn to warn them
Speed up to clear the junction first
questions.explain: At a junction you should give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross a road into which or from which you're turning.

questions.q: An ambulance with flashing blue lights and siren is coming up behind you. What should you do?
options: Find a safe place to let it pass, without breaking traffic laws
Mount the pavement to make room
Drive through the red light ahead to clear the way
questions.explain: Think about the emergency vehicle's route and help it pass, but don't put other people in danger or break the law. Avoid harsh braking or mounting the kerb.

questions.q: Another driver behaves badly and makes a rude gesture at you. What should you do?
options: Stay calm and don't get involved
Follow them to find out why
Gesture back to show them how it feels
questions.explain: Rule 147: don't let yourself get agitated or involved when someone else behaves badly on the road.

questions.q: What is the minimum legal tyre tread depth for a car?
options: 1.6 mm across the central three-quarters of the tread, around the whole tyre
1 mm across the full width of the tread
2 mm on the outer edges only
3 mm across the central half of the tread
questions.explain: Car tyres must have at least 1.6 mm of tread across the central three-quarters of the tread width, all the way round.

questions.q: Your car has anti-lock brakes (ABS). How should you brake in an emergency?
options: Press the brake pedal firmly and keep pressing until you've slowed down enough
Pump the brake pedal on and off
Pull the parking brake as well
questions.explain: Apply the footbrake firmly and don't release the pressure. ABS stops the wheels locking, so you can still steer.

questions.q: In Great Britain, when does a car normally need its first MOT test?
questions.explain: Cars must normally have their first MOT when they're three years old (four years in Northern Ireland), then every year after that.

questions.q: Who is legally responsible for making sure a 12-year-old passenger wears a seat belt?
options: The child's parent, even if they aren't in the car
Nobody, because seat belts are optional for children
questions.explain: The driver must make sure all children under 14 wear seat belts or sit in an approved child restraint.

questions.q: What is a danger of 'coasting' (driving along with the clutch pressed down or in neutral)?
options: You lose engine braking, so you have less control
It turns off your brake lights
questions.explain: Coasting removes engine braking. Your speed builds quickly downhill, the footbrake has to work harder, and steering and gear selection are affected.

questions.q: You're stopped on a public road and expect to be stationary for some time. What should you do?
options: Keep the engine running so the car stays warm
Rev the engine occasionally to keep the battery charged
Leave the engine running and get out
questions.explain: You must not leave an engine running unnecessarily while stationary on a public road. It causes pollution and wastes fuel.

questions.q: You've just driven through a flood. What should you do first?
options: Test your brakes at the first safe opportunity
Drive faster to dry out the engine
questions.explain: Wet brakes can be less effective. Test them gently at the first safe opportunity.

questions.q: What is the typical overall stopping distance for a car at 30 mph?
questions.explain: At 30 mph: about 9 m thinking distance plus 14 m braking distance, so 23 m in total.

questions.q: What is the typical overall stopping distance for a car at 70 mph on a dry road?
questions.explain: At 70 mph: about 21 m thinking distance plus 75 m braking distance, so 96 m in total. 73 m is the figure for 60 mph.

questions.q: What is the typical overall stopping distance at 50 mph?
questions.explain: At 50 mph: about 15 m thinking distance plus 38 m braking distance, so 53 m in total.

questions.q: On a wet road, how should your gap to the vehicle in front compare with the two-second gap you'd leave on a dry road?
questions.explain: Leave at least a two-second gap on dry, high-speed roads. Double it on wet roads. On icy roads it can need to be up to ten times greater.

questions.q: On icy roads, how much longer can stopping distances be compared with dry roads?
options: No longer if you have ABS
questions.explain: Stopping distances can be up to ten times greater on ice. Keep well back and brake very gently.

questions.q: You're driving in heavy rain and the steering suddenly feels light and unresponsive. What should you do?
options: Ease off the accelerator and slow down gradually
Accelerate to push through the water
questions.explain: Unresponsive steering usually means water is stopping the tyres gripping the road (aquaplaning). Ease off and slow down gradually.

questions.q: When must you use headlights during the day?
options: When visibility is seriously reduced, generally when you can't see more than 100 metres
Never, because daytime running lights are enough
questions.explain: You must use headlights when visibility is seriously reduced, generally when you can't see for more than 100 metres (328 feet).

questions.q: You've been using fog lights. The fog clears and visibility improves. What must you do?
options: Leave them on in case the fog returns
Switch to full beam as well
Switch them off only when you reach a built-up area
questions.explain: Fog lights dazzle other road users and can hide your brake lights. You must switch them off when visibility improves.

questions.q: When driving in fog, what should you be able to do?
options: Pull up well within the distance you can see clearly
Follow the rear lights of the vehicle in front closely
Use full-beam headlights to see further
questions.explain: Drive slowly enough to stop within the distance you can see clearly. Following someone's rear lights can give a false sense of security.

questions.q: A ball bounces into the road ahead from between parked cars. What should you do?
options: Slow down and be ready to stop, because a child may run out after it
Steer round the ball and carry on
Sound your horn and keep going
Speed up to get past quickly
questions.explain: Where there's a ball, there's often a child chasing it. Drive carefully and slowly when passing parked vehicles in residential areas.

questions.q: A bus has stopped at a bus stop on your side of the road. What hazard should you look out for most?
options: Pedestrians stepping out from in front of the bus
The bus's hazard lights dazzling you
questions.explain: People getting off a bus often cross the road from in front of it, where you can't see them. Go slowly and be ready to stop.

questions.q: You're approaching a zebra crossing. The car in front has stopped to let pedestrians cross. What must you NOT do?
options: Wait for the pedestrians to finish crossing
questions.explain: You must not overtake the moving vehicle nearest the crossing, or the vehicle nearest the crossing that has stopped to give way to pedestrians. It may be hiding someone who's crossing.

questions.q: A school crossing patrol shows a 'Stop for children' sign. What must you do?
options: Slow down and continue if no children are on the road yet
Sound your horn to let them know you're coming
Give way only if children are already crossing
questions.explain: You must stop when a school crossing patrol shows a 'Stop for children' sign.

questions.q: You want to pull out of a junction. When should you join the main road?
options: Only when there's a gap large enough to do so safely
As soon as the vehicle on the main road flashes its lights
When you've waited for more than 30 seconds
When traffic from the right has passed, without looking left
questions.explain: Look all around before you emerge. Don't cross or join a road until there's a gap large enough for you to do so safely.

questions.q: Why should you take extra care when emerging from a junction where there might be motorcyclists?
options: They can be hard to see and may be closer or faster than you think
They always have priority at junctions
They are not allowed to brake suddenly
They must ride in the centre of the lane
questions.explain: Motorcyclists and cyclists can be hidden by other vehicles or road features, and they could be approaching faster than you think.

questions.q: At speeds of up to 30 mph, how much space should you leave when overtaking a cyclist?
questions.explain: Leave at least 1.5 metres when overtaking cyclists at speeds of up to 30 mph, and more at higher speeds.

questions.q: How should you pass a horse rider on the road?
options: Slowly, at no more than 10 mph, leaving at least 2 metres
Quickly, so you spend less time alongside
Sounding your horn first so they know you're there
Leaving at least 1 metre at 20 mph
questions.explain: Slow down to a maximum of 10 mph, pass wide and slow with at least 2 metres of space, and don't sound your horn or rev your engine.

questions.q: You see a pedestrian with a white cane that has a red band. What does this mean?
options: They are a road safety officer
They are about to cross at a zebra crossing
questions.explain: A white cane with a red band shows that the person may be both deaf and blind. Take extra care and give them plenty of time.

questions.q: You've parked at the side of the road. What's the safest way for the driver to open their door?
options: Use the hand on the opposite side to the door (the 'Dutch Reach')
Push the door open quickly and get out
Open it slightly and wait for someone to pass
Use whichever hand is nearest the door
questions.explain: Opening the door with your far hand makes you turn your body, so you naturally look back for cyclists, motorcyclists and pedestrians.

questions.q: You're turning left at a junction and a cyclist is going straight ahead on your left. What should you do?
options: Give way and don't cut across them
Turn first, because you're in front
Indicate and carry on, because they should give way
questions.explain: Don't cut across cyclists, horse riders or horse-drawn vehicles going ahead when you're turning into or out of a junction or changing lane.

questions.q: Why should you drive more slowly near elderly, disabled or young pedestrians?
options: At 20 mph a pedestrian hit by a car is far less likely to be killed than at higher speeds
It's always the law to drive at 10 mph near pedestrians
So they can read your number plate
questions.explain: Lower speeds give you more time to react and greatly reduce injury. Rule 207 notes only a 1 in 20 chance of a pedestrian being killed at 20 mph.

questions.q: A long vehicle ahead is signalling left but moving out to the right as it approaches a junction. What should you do?
options: Stay well back and give it room to turn
questions.explain: Large vehicles often need extra road space to turn. Hang back and don't try to pass on either side.

questions.q: A bus is signalling to pull away from a bus stop just ahead of you. What should you do?
options: Give way to it if you can do so safely
Speed up to pass before it moves
Sound your horn to warn the driver
Flash your headlights so it waits
questions.explain: Give priority to buses and trams signalling to pull away from stops when you can do so safely.

questions.q: Before overtaking a large vehicle, what's most important to check?
options: That you have enough room to finish the overtake before committing to it
That the large vehicle has its lights on
That you're in the highest gear
That the driver has seen you in their mirror
questions.explain: Overtaking long vehicles takes more time and road. Make sure there's enough room to finish before you commit. Dropping back first also helps you see the road ahead.

questions.q: Why do you need to take particular care around trams?
options: They can't steer to avoid you
They always travel faster than cars
They give way to all other traffic
questions.explain: Trams run on fixed rails, so they can't swerve around you. They're also quiet and can take a long distance to stop.

questions.q: The rear of your car starts to skid to the right. What should you do?
questions.explain: Steer in the direction of the skid. If the rear skids to the right, steer right to recover. Don't brake harshly.

questions.q: How should you drive in snow or on ice?
options: At a slow speed, in as high a gear as possible, braking and accelerating gently
In a low gear with high revs for more grip
At normal speed with ABS switched on
Close behind other vehicles so you can follow their tracks
questions.explain: Drive slowly in as high a gear as possible, and accelerate, brake and steer very gently to avoid skidding.

questions.q: Your caravan starts to snake (swerve from side to side). What should you do?
options: Ease off the accelerator and reduce speed gently
Steer sharply in the opposite direction
questions.explain: Ease off and slow down gently to regain control. Don't brake harshly.

questions.q: When can a learner car driver drive on a motorway?
options: With an approved driving instructor (ADI), in a car with dual controls showing L plates
With any full licence holder over 21
Never, until they've passed their test
Only in the left lane, with any supervisor
questions.explain: Provisional car licence holders must not drive on a motorway unless accompanied by a DVSA approved driving instructor, in a car with dual controls displaying red L plates.

questions.q: A red X is shown above your lane on a motorway. What does it mean?
options: You must not drive in that lane
The lane ahead is reserved for buses
questions.explain: A red X means the lane is closed. There may be a stopped vehicle, debris or people ahead. Move to an open lane in good time.

questions.q: On a motorway with three lanes, which lane should you normally drive in?
options: The left lane, unless you're overtaking
Any lane, as long as you keep to the speed limit
The right lane, if it's clear
questions.explain: Keep to the left lane unless you're overtaking. Move back to the left when it's safe to do so.

questions.q: Which of these must NOT use the right-hand lane of a motorway with three or more lanes (except in special circumstances)?
questions.explain: Vehicles towing trailers, goods vehicles over 7.5 tonnes and certain other large vehicles must not use the right-hand lane of a motorway with three or more lanes.

questions.q: Your car breaks down on the motorway and you pull onto the hard shoulder. How should you get out?
options: By the side furthest from traffic, if it's safe, then wait well away from the vehicle
Through the driver's door, then stand behind the car
Stay in the car with the seatbelt off
Get out and walk to the nearest exit
questions.explain: Exit by the side furthest from traffic if it's safe and possible. Wait well away from your vehicle and moving traffic, behind the safety barrier if there is one.

questions.q: On a motorway, what colour are the reflective studs between the hard shoulder (or left edge) and the carriageway?
questions.explain: Red studs mark the left edge, amber the central reservation, white the lanes, and green the edge of the main carriageway at slip roads and lay-bys.

questions.q: What colour are the reflective studs that mark the edge of a slip road where it joins the main carriageway?
questions.explain: Green studs mark the edge of the main carriageway at lay-bys and slip roads.

questions.q: What is the national speed limit for cars on a motorway?
questions.explain: Cars and motorcycles: 30 mph in built-up areas, 60 on single carriageways, 70 on dual carriageways and motorways, unless signs show otherwise.

questions.q: At a roundabout, who should you normally give priority to?
questions.explain: Give priority to traffic approaching from your right, unless signs, road markings or traffic lights tell you otherwise.

questions.q: When may you enter a yellow box junction?
options: When your exit road or lane is clear
Whenever the traffic light is green
questions.explain: You must not enter the box until your exit is clear. You may enter and wait when turning right if you're only stopped by oncoming traffic or other vehicles waiting to turn right.

questions.q: The traffic light ahead changes from green to amber. When may you keep going?
options: Only if you've already crossed the stop line or are so close that stopping might cause a collision
Whenever no other traffic is around
If you speed up to get through quickly
questions.explain: Amber means stop, unless you've already crossed the stop line or are so close that stopping might cause a collision.

questions.q: Unless in an authorised parking space, how close to a junction must you NOT park?
questions.explain: Don't stop or park opposite or within 10 metres (32 feet) of a junction, except in an authorised parking space.

questions.q: You're parking on a road at night, not in a recognised parking space. Which way must your car face?
options: In the direction of the traffic flow
Against the direction of traffic flow
Either way, as long as your lights are on
Whichever way is easiest to leave
questions.explain: You must not park on a road at night facing against the direction of the traffic flow, unless you're in a recognised parking space.

questions.q: Which of these should you never do?
options: Reverse from a side road into a main road
Reverse around a corner into a quiet side road
Reverse for a short distance in a car park
questions.explain: Don't reverse from a side road into a main road. Reverse into the side road instead, so you emerge forwards.

questions.q: At a pelican crossing the amber light is flashing and a pedestrian is still on the crossing. What must you do?
options: Drive on, because flashing amber means go
Sound your horn to hurry them
questions.explain: When the amber light is flashing you must give way to any pedestrians on the crossing.

questions.q: Who can use a toucan crossing?
questions.explain: Toucan crossings are light-controlled crossings that let cyclists and pedestrians share the crossing space and cross at the same time.

questions.q: What is the national speed limit for a car on a single carriageway road?
questions.explain: For cars: 30 mph in built-up areas, 60 mph on single carriageways, 70 mph on dual carriageways and motorways, unless signs show otherwise.

questions.q: There are double white lines in the centre of the road and the line nearest you is solid. When may you cross it to overtake?
options: To pass a cyclist, horse rider or road maintenance vehicle travelling at 10 mph or less, if safe
Whenever the road ahead is clear
questions.explain: You must not cross or straddle a solid line on your side, except when it's safe and you need to enter premises or a side road, or to pass a stationary vehicle, or a cyclist, horse rider or road maintenance vehicle doing 10 mph or less.

questions.q: When may you use hazard warning lights while driving?
options: On a motorway or unrestricted dual carriageway, briefly, to warn drivers behind of a hazard ahead
When you're parked on double yellow lines
When driving slowly in bad weather
questions.explain: Hazard lights may be used while stationary to warn that you're temporarily obstructing traffic. You must not use them while driving, except on a motorway or unrestricted dual carriageway to warn of a hazard ahead.

questions.q: What does this sign mean?
questions.imageAlt: Inverted red-bordered white triangle with the words GIVE WAY
options: Give way to traffic on the major road
Stop at the line in all cases
questions.explain: The inverted triangle is the 'give way' sign. It has a unique shape so it can be recognised even when covered in snow or dirt.

questions.q: What must you do at this sign?
questions.imageAlt: Red octagonal sign with the word STOP
options: Stop at the line, then give way to traffic on the major road
Slow down and give way if necessary
Stop only if traffic is coming
Stop only if a police officer is present
questions.explain: The octagonal STOP sign means you must stop completely at the line, even if the road looks clear, then give way.

questions.q: What does this sign mean?
questions.imageAlt: Red circle with a horizontal white bar
questions.explain: A red circle with a white bar means no entry for vehicles. You'll usually see it at the exit end of a one-way street.

questions.q: What does this sign mean?
questions.imageAlt: White circle with a black diagonal stripe
options: End of all restrictions, so there's no speed limit
questions.explain: The white circle with a black diagonal stripe means the national speed limit for that type of road and vehicle applies. It never means there's no limit.

questions.q: What does this sign mean?
questions.imageAlt: Blue circle with red border and a red diagonal cross
questions.explain: A red cross on a blue background with a red border means no stopping at all during the times shown, not even to set down or pick up passengers.

questions.q: What does this sign mean?
questions.imageAlt: Blue circle with red border and a single red diagonal line
options: No parking for disabled badge holders
questions.explain: A single red diagonal bar means no waiting. Compare it with the red cross (no stopping). Times are usually shown on a plate below.

questions.q: What does this sign mean?
questions.imageAlt: Blue circle with the white number 30
questions.explain: Blue circles give positive (mandatory) instructions. A blue circle with a number shows a minimum speed. A red ring with a number shows a maximum.

questions.q: What does this sign mean?
questions.imageAlt: White circle with red border and the number 30
questions.explain: A red ring means prohibition. Here, you must not exceed 30 mph.

questions.q: What does this sign mean?
questions.imageAlt: Blue circle with a white arrow pointing up
questions.explain: Blue circles give mandatory instructions. This one means you may only go straight ahead.

questions.q: Signs that give orders are mostly what shape?
questions.explain: Circles give orders, triangles warn, and rectangles inform. The exceptions are STOP (octagon) and GIVE WAY (inverted triangle).

questions.q: What do triangular signs (pointing upwards) generally do?
options: Show the route to a motorway
questions.explain: Triangular signs are warnings. Circles give orders and rectangles give information.

questions.q: Someone supervising a learner car driver must be at least what age, and have held a full car licence for how long?
options: 21, and held a full licence for at least 3 years
18, and held a full licence for at least 1 year
25, and held a full licence for at least 5 years
questions.explain: A supervisor must be at least 21 and have held a full licence for that category of vehicle for at least 3 years.

questions.q: You passed your driving test 18 months ago. How many penalty points would lead to your licence being revoked?
questions.explain: Under the New Drivers Act, if you get 6 or more points within two years of passing your first test, your licence is revoked and you must re-take your tests.

questions.q: What is the minimum level of insurance cover you must have to drive on the road?
questions.explain: To use a vehicle on the road you must be covered at least for third party liability.

questions.q: In good daylight, from what distance must you be able to read a vehicle number plate (with glasses or contact lenses if you need them)?
questions.explain: You must be able to read a vehicle number plate in good daylight from 20 metres, using glasses or contact lenses if you need them.

questions.q: In England and Wales, what is the legal blood alcohol limit for driving?
questions.explain: In England and Wales the limit is 80 mg alcohol per 100 ml of blood (35 µg per 100 ml of breath). Scotland's limits are lower. The safest choice is not to drink at all if you're driving.

questions.q: You've broken down on an ordinary road. How far behind your vehicle should you place a warning triangle?
questions.explain: Place a warning triangle at least 45 metres (147 feet) behind your vehicle on the same side of the road. Never use one on a motorway.

questions.q: You're involved in a collision and don't give your name and address at the scene. Within what time must you report it to the police?
options: As soon as reasonably practicable, and in any case within 24 hours
questions.explain: If you don't give your details at the time, report the collision to the police as soon as reasonably practicable, and in any case within 24 hours.

questions.q: An injured motorcyclist is lying in the road. What should you NOT do?
options: Remove their helmet, unless it's essential
questions.explain: Don't remove a motorcyclist's helmet unless it's essential, for example if they're not breathing normally. You could make a spinal injury worse.

questions.q: At an incident, someone has a burn. How long should you cool it with clean, cool water?
options: Until the pain stops, even if it's under a minute
questions.explain: Cool the burn for at least 20 minutes with plenty of clean, cool water. Don't remove anything that's sticking to the burn.

questions.q: When giving chest compressions to an adult, how deep and how fast should you press?
options: About 5 to 6 cm, about twice a second
About 1 to 2 cm, once every 2 seconds
As gently as possible, about once every 5 seconds
questions.explain: Press down hard and fast, around 5 to 6 centimetres deep and about twice a second.

questions.q: In first aid, what does 'DR ABC' stand for?
questions.explain: Check for Danger, check for a Response, open the Airway, check Breathing, then deal with Circulation (bleeding and compressions).

questions.q: You're first to arrive at a crash. What should you ask the drivers involved to do?
options: Switch off their engines and stop smoking
Move their vehicles to the side straight away
Keep their engines running for heat
Leave the scene before the police arrive
questions.explain: Ask drivers to switch off their engines and everyone to stop smoking, because there may be spilt fuel. Then call the emergency services.

questions.q: Your car stalls on a level crossing. What should you do first?
options: Get everyone out of the vehicle and clear of the crossing
Keep trying to restart the engine
Walk down the line to look for a train
Push the car off the crossing straight away
questions.explain: Get everyone out and clear of the crossing immediately. Then use the railway telephone, if there is one, to tell the signal operator. Only try to move the car if there's plenty of time.

questions.q: At a level crossing, a train has just passed but the red lights keep flashing. What must you do?
options: Keep waiting, because another train is coming
Cross carefully now the train has gone
questions.explain: You must wait if a train goes by and the red lights keep flashing. It means another train will be passing soon.

questions.q: Who is responsible for making sure a vehicle isn't overloaded?
options: The vehicle's owner, even when they aren't driving
questions.explain: You must not overload your vehicle or trailer. As the driver, you're responsible.

questions.q: You're carrying a load on a roof rack. What must you make sure of?
options: It's secure and doesn't stick out dangerously
It's no taller than the car
questions.explain: You must secure your load and it must not stick out dangerously. Heavy or sharp objects and any animals must be secured safely.

questions.q: Where must a rear-facing baby seat NOT be fitted?
options: In a seat protected by an active frontal airbag
In any seat with a three-point seat belt
questions.explain: An active frontal airbag can seriously injure or kill a baby in a rear-facing seat in a crash.

questions.q: How should the load be arranged in a caravan or trailer?
options: Spread evenly, to reduce the risk of snaking
As much as possible at the very back
It doesn't matter if it's secure
questions.explain: Spreading the weight evenly reduces the risk of swerving or snaking and losing control.

questions.q: You're taking your dog on a car journey. What should you do?
options: Let it sit on the front passenger's lap
Let it roam free so it stays calm
Open a window fully so it can put its head out
questions.explain: Make sure dogs and other animals are suitably restrained, so they can't distract you or be hurt if you stop quickly.
